title: Shortest Path in a Binary Grid
statement:
An ad delivery service models a data centre floor as an n x n grid of racks. A request must travel from the rack in the top-left corner to the rack in the bottom-right corner, hopping between neighbouring racks. Some racks are down for maintenance and cannot be used.

The grid is a list of n strings, each of length n. grid[r][c] is '0' if that rack is open and '1' if it is blocked. From an open cell you can move to any of its 8 neighbours (up, down, left, right and the 4 diagonals) if that neighbour is open and inside the grid.

Write def solution(grid) that returns the number of cells on the shortest path from (0, 0) to (n - 1, n - 1), counting both ends. Return -1 if there is no such path, including when the start or the end cell is blocked. A 1 x 1 open grid returns 1.

examples.why: The LeetCode 1091 example 1. One diagonal step: 2 cells.
The LeetCode 1091 example 2. (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 2): the middle hop is diagonal.
The LeetCode 1091 example 3. The start cell is blocked, so there is no path at all.

think.q: What does the answer count, and what are the moves?
think.a: It counts cells, not moves: a path of k moves has k + 1 cells. Each move goes to one of 8 neighbours, so a diagonal step costs the same as a side step. Every move costs 1, which is the property the right algorithm depends on.

think.q: Find the answer for ["000", "110", "110"] by growing rings outward from the start.
think.a: Ring 1: {(0, 0)}. Ring 2: its open neighbours, {(0, 1)}. Ring 3: new open neighbours of ring 2, {(0, 2), (1, 2)}. Ring 4: {(2, 2)}, the target. So the answer is 4. You never needed to try a path twice: the ring a cell first appears in is its distance.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Give every cell a distance of 'infinity' except the start (1), then sweep the whole grid over and over, lowering each neighbour to dist + 1 when that is smaller, until a sweep changes nothing. It is correct, but a winding maze needs one sweep per bend: O(cells^2). Trying every path with DFS is worse: exponential.

Breadth-first search. When every move costs the same, BFS explores cells in order of distance: all cells at distance d leave the queue before any cell at distance d + 1. So the first time BFS reaches a cell, it got there along a shortest path, and it never needs to revisit it. That is O(cells x 8).

1. If grid[0][0] or grid[n-1][n-1] is '1', return -1.
  2. dist = n x n of 0 (0 = not reached); dist[0][0] = 1; deque with (0, 0).
  3. Pop a cell. If it is the target, return its dist.
  4. For each of the 8 offsets: if the neighbour is in bounds, open and unreached, set its dist to this cell's + 1 and enqueue it.
  5. When the queue is empty, return -1.

Start blocked, end blocked. A 1 x 1 open grid (answer 1, not 0) and a 1 x 1 blocked grid. A wall that cuts the grid in two. A path that only exists through a diagonal gap between two blocked cells. An open grid, where the answer is n because diagonals are allowed. A serpentine maze where the path is much longer than n.

hints: Every move costs 1, so the shortest path is the one with the fewest moves. Which traversal visits cells in order of how many moves away they are?
BFS from (0, 0) with a deque. Store each cell's distance (in cells) when you first reach it; the start is 1, not 0.
Mark a cell when you enqueue it, so it is never queued twice. The 8 moves are every (dr, dc) with dr, dc in -1, 0, 1 except (0, 0). Check both corners before you start.
explain:
Example 2, ["000", "110", "110"]:

  • Start: dist[0][0] = 1, queue = [(0, 0)].
  • Pop (0, 0). Open, unreached neighbours: (0, 1). Set it to 2. (1, 0) and (1, 1) are blocked.
  • Pop (0, 1). New neighbours: (0, 2) and (1, 2), both set to 3.
  • Pop (0, 2): nothing new. Pop (1, 2): (2, 2) set to 4.
  • Pop (2, 2): it is the target, return 4.

Why BFS and not DFS: the queue is first in, first out, so it always holds cells of distance d followed by cells of distance d + 1. A cell's first visit therefore comes along a shortest route, and the target's first pop is the answer. A DFS follows one direction as deep as it can, so the first path it finds to the target can be far longer than the best one; making DFS exact means trying every path. If the moves had different costs, BFS would stop being exact and you would switch to Dijkstra with heapq.
complexity: O(n^2) time (each cell is enqueued once and checks 8 neighbours), O(n^2) extra space

al.from: LC 1091 Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
talk: Why BFS gives the shortest path: every move costs 1, and a FIFO deque pops all cells at distance d before any at d + 1. So the first time I reach a cell, no shorter route to it exists, and the first time I pop the target I can return.

Why not DFS: DFS commits to one direction, so the first path it finds is just a path. To make DFS exact I would have to try every path (exponential) or keep re-relaxing cells, which is the slow sweep version.
I set dist when I enqueue, not when I pop; otherwise one cell can enter the queue up to 8 times. The dist grid doubles as the visited set, with 0 meaning unreached.
Off-by-one: the answer counts cells, so the start is 1. I check both corners up front, which also makes the 1 x 1 cases fall out: ["0"] is 1 and ["1"] is -1.
O(n^2) time and space: each cell is enqueued once and looks at 8 offsets, kept in one list of (dr, dc) pairs.
extensions: Return the path itself, not just its length: store a parent for each cell when you enqueue it, then walk back from the target.
Racks have different hop costs (latency in ms): why does BFS stop being exact, and how does Dijkstra with heapq fix it?
Speed it up on a 10,000 x 10,000 floor: bidirectional BFS from both corners, or A* with the Chebyshev distance max(|dr|, |dc|) as the heuristic.
You may unblock up to k racks (LC 1293): make the BFS state (r, c, removals_left).
Only 4-directional moves are allowed: what changes in the code, and what is example 1's answer then?
